claims.text: Oxide-scale spallation and morphological instability at elevated temperature are the primary drivers of corrosion failure in Q235 steel.
At room to moderately elevated temperatures, Q235 steel can form a more adherent oxide film that maintains protection in aggressive salt environments.
As-received Q235 has a typical low-carbon-steel microstructure and a thin native oxide layer.
A controlled study should expose Q235 and a reference boiler steel from room temperature to approximately 900 °C under fixed salt chemistry, oxygen partial pressure, and dwell times.
Oxide-scale adherence, thickness, and compositional integrity are the proposed structural mediators of protection.
At lower temperatures, the oxide film formed on Q235 remains coherent and passivates the steel in salt environments.
Above approximately 700 °C, Q235 oxide scales become susceptible to cracking and spallation.
Thermal stresses promote cracking and spallation of the Q235 oxide scale above approximately 700 °C.
Accelerated oxide growth promotes cracking and spallation of the Q235 oxide scale above approximately 700 °C.
Aggressive salts destabilize the Q235 oxide scale and promote its spallation at high temperature.
Spallation exposes underlying steel to corrosive species, causing rapid local corrosion and loss of protection.
Q235 will show relatively mild corrosion and a coherent oxide scale at lower and moderate temperatures.
Beyond approximately 700 °C in salt-laden environments, Q235 will show increased spallation, mass loss, and pit or scale damage.
A corrosion-resistant boiler-steel reference will exhibit more stable high-temperature oxide layers, less spallation, and lower mass loss than Q235.
Below approximately 700 °C, Q235's passive oxide remains relatively intact.
Lower chloride activity or lower oxidation potential should reduce oxide-scale failure in Q235.
Processing history, surface finish, and local microstructure may shift the temperature at which Q235 scale destabilizes.
A coherent, non-spalling Q235 oxide scale with no accelerated corrosion through 900 °C in the specified salt environment would falsify the proposed mechanism under those conditions.
